newsitem.title: PERU: Amid uncertainty, Peru crisis enters 81st day.
newsitem.headline: Amid uncertainty, Peru crisis enters 81st day.

text.p: With talks to free them stalled, 72 men held by Marxist rebels in Peru began on Saturday their 81st day in captivity amid growing uncertainty, despite President Alberto Fujimori's assurances he wants a bloodless end to the crisis.
Fujimori said in a statement on Friday that he would use "a humanitarian sense" and seek to resolve Latin America's longest hostage crisis by peaceful means.

But he dodged reporters' questions about rebel charges, backed by news reports, that security forces were digging tunnels to storm the Japanese ambassador's home and left open the possibility of a violent solution if hostages are harmed.
The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) hostage-takers abruptly called off Friday's scheduled face-to-face meeting with the government.
They cited burrowing noises coming from under the building's floor and charged the government planned to attack the compound.
But Fujimori assured members of a guarantors commission mediating the talks, who met with him on Friday that he still wanted a peaceful outcome.
"We have received the express confirmation of this very same intention from the president in a meeting," Vatican representative Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani said in a statement read to reporters.

Cipriani, a member of the three-man mediating panel, noted that Fujimori and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto had agreed in Canada last month to seek a peaceful solution to the crisis and prevent loss of life.

But Fujimori on Friday did not rule out the use of force if hostages were harmed, saying the bloodless path would be followed only as long as the MRTA "fully respected the life and health of the hostages."
"The state, in consequence, will stay alert at all times to any change in this scenario," the statement said.

Fujimori, still smarting from the rebels' rejection of his offer to allow them asylum in Cuba, huddled with his negotiators on Friday to map their next move, meeting twice with his chief negotiator, Domingo Palermo.
Nine meetings between the government and rebels since face- to-face talks restarted Feb. 11 had brought progress toward ending the crisis, with both sides laying out formal proposals on Wednesday.
But the MRTA refused to attend the tenth round, set for Friday, dashing optimism for a peaceful solution and heightening tension in the standoff.
Peruvian Defence Minister Tomas Castillo Meza denied the existence of the tunnels, but Lima newspapers were full of precise details of where and how they were being built.
One report, citing state sources, gave the address of the building where one tunnel supposedly began and said it would lead into the compound's kitchen or dining room.
Japan appealed to the rebels to reconsider their stand.

"The Japanese government strongly supports efforts ... to secure the safe release of all the hostages," government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told reporters. "Therefore, we hope the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement side will attend the next round of preliminary dialogue."
The rebels have been holding the hostages, including Fujimori's brother, Pedro, and two cabinet ministers, since Dec. 17 in the spacious diplomatic compound in Lima's swank San Isidro neighbourhood.

On Thursday, rebel leader Nestor Cerpa said he had evidence the government aimed to rescue the hostages while he and his second-in-command, Rolly Rojas, attended talks at a safe house across the street from the diplomatic residence.

Security force sources consulted by Reuters confirmed that at least four tunnels had been dug under the compound in recent weeks. The tunnels would be used if there was an attack, which would last seven minutes and cause many deaths, they added.
